Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 101, verses 1–3:

Tafsir of Surah "Al-Qari'ah" (The Striking Calamity). It is Meccan by consensus, and it has ten verses. [In the book Ruh al-Ma'ani: its verses number eleven in the Kufan reckoning, ten in the Hijazi, and eight in the Basran and Syrian.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The Striking Calamity! What is the Striking Calamity? And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Striking Calamity! What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ means the Resurrection and the Hour. So said most of the exegetes. This is because it strikes creation with its terrors and frights. The lexicographers say: the Arabs say, "The calamity struck them (qaraʿathum al-qari'ah)" and "the disaster broke their backs (faqarathum al-faqirah)," when a dreadful matter befalls them. Ibn Ahmar said:

"And a striking calamity from the days, were it not for their way, would have moved away from you for a while."

Another said:

"Whenever your flint (al-marwah, a stone from which fire is struck) strikes, it troubles you, and no fire is kindled for us in the cooking pot."

And He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And disaster will not cease to strike those who disbelieve for what they have done﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31] and it is the most severe of the hardships of time.

His saying: ﴿What is the Striking Calamity?﴾ is an interrogative, meaning: what is the Striking Calamity? Likewise, "And what will make you know what the Striking Calamity is?" is a question in the manner of magnifying and exalting its matter, as He said: "The Inevitable Reality! What is the Inevitable Reality? And what will make you know what the Inevitable Reality is?" [al-Haqqah: 1–3], as previously discussed [see vol. 18, p. 257].

Mansub as an adverbial of time (ẓarf); its implied sense is: "The Striking Calamity will occur on the day when people will be like scattered moths." Qatadah said: al-farash is the insects that fall into fire and lamps. Its singular is farashah, and Abu 'Ubaydah said the same. Al-Farra' said: it is the swarming flying insects, from gnats and others, and among them the locust. It is said: "He is more flighty (atyash) than a moth." And a poet said:

Tuwayyish min nafar atyash... atyash min ta'irat al-farash
(A little one among a band of flighty ones... more flighty than a flying moth)

Another poet said:

"And there were folk whose hearts I turned back to them [[In some copies: (upon them).]], and they were like moths in their ignorance."

In the Sahih of Muslim, on the authority of Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My likeness and your likeness is like the likeness of a man who kindled a fire, and the grasshoppers and moths began to fall into it, while he was warding them off from it. And I am taking hold of your waistbands away from the Fire, while you slip out of my hand." And there is a related narration on the authority of Abu Hurayrah. Al-mabthuth means the scattered. And in another place He said: "As if they were scattered locusts" [[Verse 7, Surah al-Qamar.]] [al-Qamar: 7]. So their initial state is like moths, having no direction, bewildered in every direction; then they become like locusts, because the locust has a direction it aims for. Al-mabthuth: the dispersed and the spread out. It was mentioned in the masculine according to the wording, as in His saying: "Trunks of uprooted palm trees" [[Verse 20, Surah al-Qamar.]] [al-Qamar: 20]. Had it said al-mabthutha [it would be [[Addition from Tafsir Ibn Adil, required by the context.]]], as in His saying: "Trunks of hollow palm trees" [[Verse 7, Surah al-Haqqah.]] [al-Haqqah: 7]. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Farra' said: "Like scattered moths" means like the swarming locusts, some of which mount others. So too will people be, surging among one another when they are raised.

Like wool that is carded by hand, meaning it becomes dust-like scattered particles and vanishes, as He, exalted is His praise, said in another place: ﴿scattered dust particles﴾ [[Verse 6 of Surah al-Waqi'ah.]] [al-Waqi'ah: 6]. The lexicographers say: al-'Ihn is dyed wool. This has already been discussed in Surah (Sa'ala sa'il) [[See vol. 18, p. 284.]].

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*) on Surah 101, verses 6–11:

The discussion of the scale (*al-mizan*) has already passed in "al-A'raf," "al-Kahf," and "al-Anbiya'" [[See vol. 7, p. 165 and following. And vol. 11, p. 66 and p. (293)]]. It has a pan and a tongue, and in it are weighed the scrolls on which the good deeds and the bad deeds are written. It was said: it is one scale, held in the hand of Jibril, which weighs the deeds of the children of Adam, so it was expressed with the word in the plural form (*mawazin*?). Others said: there are many scales, as the poet said:

*"Malikun taqumu al-hadithatu li-'adlihi"*
[The first line of the verse:]
"A King by whose justice all events stand..."

We have mentioned this in what preceded [[See vol. 11, p. (293)]]. We have also mentioned it in the book *al-Tadhkira*. It was said: the scales are the proofs and the arguments. This was said by 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Yahya, and he cited the words of the poet:

*"Qad kuntu qabla liqa'ikum dha mirratin... 'indi li-kulli mukhasimin mizanuhu"*

As for the meaning of ﴿in a pleasing life﴾, it means a life that is pleasing, which its owner is content with. It was also said: ﴿a pleasing life﴾ means a life that causes contentment, that is, gentleness and submission to its people. The verb is attributed to the life because it gives contentment from itself, which is gentleness and submission. The "life" is a word that gathers the blessings that are in Paradise, so it is the one that causes contentment, like the raised couches, whose height is the distance of a hundred years. When the friend of God approaches them, they lower themselves until he sits upon them, then they rise up in their former state. Likewise the tree, its branch is also raised. When the friend of God desires its fruit, it bends down to him, until the friend of God takes it, sitting or standing. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Its clusters hang low within reach﴾ [al-Haqqah: 23]. Wherever he walks or moves from place to place, a river flows along with him wherever he wishes, high and low. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They make it gush forth in abundance﴾ [al-Insan: 6]. It is reported in a narration (that he points with his staff and it flows without a trench wherever he wishes, in his palaces and in his gatherings). So all these things are a life that has given contentment from itself, and it is the one that causes contentment. It is humbled and submits, giving and generous.

As for the meaning of ﴿then his mother is the Abyss﴾, it means Hell. It is called a mother because he resorts to it as one resorts to his mother. This was said by Ibn Zayd, and from it is the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

*"Fa-l-ardu ma'qilunا wa-kanat ummana... fiha maqabiruna wa-fiha nuladu"*
"The earth is our refuge, and it was our mother; in it are our graves, and in it we are born."

Hell was named *al-Hawiyah* (the Abyss) because one falls into it with the great depth of its bottom. It is reported that *al-Hawiyah* is the name of the lowest gate of Hell. Qatadah said: the meaning of ﴿then his mother is the Abyss﴾ is that his destination is the Fire. 'Ikrimah said: because he falls into it headfirst (lit. on the top of his head). Al-Akhfash said: ﴿his mother﴾ means his dwelling place, and the meanings are close. The poet said:

*"Ya 'Umar law nalatka ar-massu ana... kunta ka-man tahwi bihi al-hawiyah"*
"O 'Umar, if our spears had reached you, you would have been like one whom the Abyss throws down."

*Al-Hawiyah* is *al-mahwah* (the pit). And you say: *hawat ummuhu*, so she is *hawiyah*, that is, bereaved, as Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi said:

*"Hawat ummuhu ma yab'athu as-subhu ghadiyan... wa-madha yu'addi al-laylu hina ya'ubu"*
"May his mother be bereaved, what does the morning send forth at dawn, and what does the night bring when it returns?"

*Al-Mahwa* and *al-Mahwah* are what lies between two mountains, and the like. And *tahawa al-qawm fi al-mahwah* means when some of them fall one after another into the pit.

(﴿And what will make you know what it is?﴾) The original is *ma hiya*, and the *ha'* was added for pausing. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Ibn Muhaysin read *ma hiya nar* without the *ha'* in connected speech, and they paused on it. Its explanation has already passed in Surah al-Haqqah [[See vol. 18, p. 269]].

(﴿A blazing Fire﴾) means of extreme heat. In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Your fire that the son of Adam kindles is one part of seventy parts of the heat of Hell." They said: "By God, it would be sufficient, O Messenger of God." He said: "It has been made superior to it by sixty-nine parts, each of which is like its heat."

It is related from Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "The scale of whoever's scale becomes heavy is heavy only because the Truth was placed in it, and it is right that a scale in which the Truth is placed should be heavy. And the scale of whoever's scale becomes light is light only because falsehood was placed in it, and it is right that a scale in which falsehood is placed should be light."

In the report from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The dead ask the man who comes to them about a man who died before him. He says: 'So-and-so died before me; did he not pass by you?' They say: 'No, by God.' He says: 'Surely to God we belong and to Him we return!' He has been taken to his mother, the Abyss. How evil is the mother, and how evil is the one who nurtures!"

We have mentioned it in full in the book *al-Tadhkira*, and praise be to God.
